column3: What did Smoot say he had ordered the U.S. ships to go back to doing?
column4: Return to normal patrol operations in the Taiwan Straits.
column5: P01-A|have directed US ships resume normal patrol operations in Taiwan Straits.

column3: What instruction connects State's telegram 304 to the notification Smoot described on October 7?
column4: State instructed the embassy to pass the statement to Chiang, and Smoot reports the ambassador was passing information from 304 to the GRC as notification regarding convoy escorts.
column5: P01-B|You should immediately pass text this statement to President Chiang
column6: P01-A|Ambassador is passing information contained in SecState 304 to GRC. This constitutes notification to GRC of action in re escort of convoy.

column3: Did Smoot describe normal patrols as ending all U.S. protection for emergencies during the lull?
column4: No. He reported a separate agreement with the Chinese Navy to arrange normal patrols to provide adequate emergency protection during the lull.
column5: P01-A|have reached agreement with Chinese Navy that our normal patrols in Straits can be arranged as to provide adequate protection for emergencies during this period of lull.

column3: Do these documents establish that Tiger and Minister Yu Ta Wei later heard about the emergency protection arrangement through their own channels?
column4: Withhold. Smoot says U.S. officials had not informed them yet and describes only the ambassador's suggested route.
column5: P01-A|Tiger [Wang and] Minister Yu Ta Wei not informed of foregoing by any US official as yet.
column6: P01-A|allow the information reach Tiger and Minister Yu Ta Wei through their own channels.

column3: Which of the three subjects did Kishi still insist on putting in the communiqué on December 24?
column4: The consultation formula.
column5: P02-A|Re consultation formula, Kishi feels he must insist that this be included in the communiqué.

column3: How did the position on including the Article III islands in the communiqué develop between the two telegrams?
column4: Washington preferred leaving specific treaty terms out and flagged Defense clearance for Article III. By December 24, MacArthur reported the Japanese side accepted an agreed minute and would drop the communiqué reference.
column5: P02-B|particularly concerned with problem obtaining Defense clearance on Article III reference in communiqué
column6: P02-A|They agree to have Article III islands in agreed minute as proposed in Deptel 1487 and will not ask for reference to Article III islands to be included in communiqué.

column3: What condition did Washington set for allowing any of the specific treaty provisions into the communiqué?
column4: The exact wording had to be agreed and frozen well in advance, with no negotiation of those terms during Kishi's visit.
column5: P02-B|unless exact language is agreed to well in advance and frozen. We are not prepared to negotiate language of communique with respect above matters during Kishi’s visit here.

column3: What wording for indirect aggression actually appeared in the final communiqué?
column4: Withhold. The telegram reports that Japan would no longer insist on inclusion and Kishi had not decided how to handle it. The final communiqué is absent.
column5: P02-A|Kishi now plans to handle this matter either by such an agreed minute, or by a unilateral statement or by simply saying nothing, although he has not yet decided which course to follow.

column3: When and where did Tyler say he had discussed the proposed coalition with British officials?
column4: In London on July 16 and 17.
column5: P03-A|During my talks in London with British officials July 16 and 17

column3: What part of Tyler's July 31 recommendation is reflected in Rusk's August 4 message to Sandys?
column4: Raise US doubts about a pre-election coalition again and ask Sandys to reconsider. The sequence is consistent with the recommendation.
column5: P03-A|reiterates our doubts about a coalition and asks for further consideration
column6: P03-B|raise again the doubts and misgivings about a pre-election coalition
column7: P03-B|give further consideration to these very real concerns on our part about the dangers of such a course of action

column3: Did Rusk say ending the sugar workers' strike had already improved security?
column4: No. He reported the strike ended and said any immediate security improvement remained to be seen.
column5: P03-B|The strike of the sugar workers has been ended in what amounts to a defeat for Jagan. Whether this will result in any immediate improvement in the security situation, of course, remains to be seen.

column3: What was the disagreement between Sandys and Tyler over a coalition before the British Guiana elections?
column4: Tyler reported that Sandys thought an all-party coalition was necessary to restore order and security. Tyler doubted the security benefit and regarded a pre-election coalition as dangerous to US political objectives.
column5: P03-A|he believes order and security in British Guiana can only be restored through an all party coalition government
column6: P03-A|was of doubtful value so far as security is concerned and dangerous from the point of view of our political objectives in British Guiana.

column3: How many of Lam Thanh Nguyen's troops did the June 3 memorandum say were covered by the integration negotiations?
column4: 3,000. The memorandum attributes the report to a redacted source.
column5: P04-B|negotiations were completed on 2 June for the integration of 3,000 of Lam Thanh Nguyen’s troops into the Vietnamese National Army.

column3: How did Young's June 1 account and the June 3 memorandum each characterize Diem's capacity to handle his immediate challenges?
column4: Young said Washington had no evidence Diem had overreached. The June 3 memorandum reported a positive assessment of his ability to handle the problems he had chosen.
column5: P04-A|there does not seem to be any evidence available in Washington at this time to indicate Diem has “bitten off more than he can chew”.
column6: P04-B|Premier Diem is believed capable of handling the problems he has chosen to attack at this time.

column3: How did Young qualify the optimistic Saigon source comment he forwarded?
column4: Young said it was not a fully evaluated report and represented only Lansdale's opinion.
column5: P04-A|Of course this is not a fully evaluated report and represents only Lansdale’s opinion.

column3: Does the packet establish that the planned military operation against Soai and Ba Cut was actually carried out?
column4: Withhold. It describes plans, their readiness and probable success if needed, with no execution record.
column5: P04-B|it will be successful if it is needed.
column6: P04-B|the plans for military moves against Soai and Ba Cut, if such steps are necessary.

column3: How long did Lodge say he spent with Eisenhower?
column4: One-half hour.
column5: P05-B|Spent one-half hour with General Eisenhower as you requested.

column3: What does Bundy report about Lodge's omission from the White Paper, and what separate activity does Lodge describe in his earlier memorandum?
column4: Bundy said it omitted Lodge's name in its discussion of Diem's last months. In the earlier August memo Lodge reported meeting Eisenhower for half an hour at Johnson's request. These are separate contexts.
column5: P05-A|this report omits the name of Ambassador Lodge in its discussion of the last months of Diem.
column6: P05-B|Spent one-half hour with General Eisenhower as you requested.

column3: When, according to Bundy's description of Johnson's 1961 report, might a commitment of troops be necessary?
column4: If circumstances changed. Bundy says Johnson's report warned a commitment might then be needed.
column5: P05-A|your farsighted report specifically warned that we might need to make a commitment of troops if circumstances should change.

column3: Can these two memoranda establish the exact words the Republican White Paper used about Laos?
column4: Withhold. Bundy characterized the impression as false. The White Paper text itself is absent and Lodge's memorandum is a separate account.
column5: P05-A|The document also conveys a false impression of your views on Laos.

column3: Which two categories of assistance did the May 3 draft say the cutoff would leave untouched?
column4: Telecommunications equipment and special forces training.
column5: P06-A|We agree telecommunications equipment and special forces training not included this cut-off.

column3: How did the May 9 telegram change the position on using aid sanctions from the May 3 draft responding to the same Saigon message?
column4: The draft proposed withholding further emergency equipment pending steps toward settling issues with Cambodia. The later telegram authorized the presentation with the aid-sanction portion removed. The draft itself does not establish a cutoff occurred.
column5: P06-A|Ref: Saigon’s 3095.
column6: P06-A|no further emergency equipment will be sent until GVN takes steps you outline
column8: P06-B|you are authorized use line set forth your reftel action paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 eliminating that portion para 3 on aid sanctions.

column3: Did removing aid sanctions from the authorized presentation mean the Department ruled out any future action over misuse of assistance?
column4: No. The telegram said the United States would seriously consider action if assistance were misused for other purposes.
column5: P06-B|should assistance which we are providing be misused for other purposes we will give serious consideration to backing our words with action.

column3: Do the draft and later telegram establish whether the six H–34 helicopters were actually delivered?
column4: Withhold. The later telegram discusses equipment for which funds were likely to be requested under a hypothetical sanction, with no delivery confirmation.
column5: P06-B|remaining emergency equipment for which DOD is likely to request funds includes only six H–34 helicopters
